iut_type: End Products (Key System smart jump rope and smart band), products not implementing an already-certified SoC
customer_question: For our smart jump rope product, we're not using an already SIG-certified Bluetooth chip (no existing QDID). What test scope and registration approach does this require?
question_variants: Why would we need to test protocol layers like Link Layer, GAP, and GATT at the product level?
Can these middle protocol layers be tested using our actual product, or do we need something else?
actual_issue: The customer's first product (a smart jump rope) was being built without any pre-certified Bluetooth chip/SoC, raising the question of what additional certification testing burden this choice would create compared to using an already-certified component.
plain_english_explanation: Bluetooth certification testing splits into layers: the lowest layer (RF PHY) and the highest layers (profiles like DIS, BAS) can be tested directly against the actual product implementation. However, the middle protocol layers — Link Layer, L2CAP, GAP, GATT, ATT, and SM — cannot be meaningfully tested against a product implementation alone; they require the product to implement an already SIG-registered SoC and Host Stack, whose existing registration covers those middle-layer test requirements. If the product doesn't implement any already-registered SoC/Host Stack combination, the manufacturer must run and report actual tests for those middle layers themselves and upload the results at registration time — a substantial undertaking. The practical recommendation is to implement an already-certified SoC plus Host Stack combination specifically to avoid this middle-layer testing burden.
consultant_answer: RF PHY and profile-layer (e.g., DIS, BAS) testing can be done directly against your actual product. But the middle protocol layers — Link Layer, L2CAP, GAP, GATT, ATT, and SM — can't be meaningfully tested at the product level alone; they require your product to implement an already SIG-registered SoC and Host Stack, whose existing registration covers those middle layers. Since your jump rope doesn't use any already-certified chip, you'd need to run and report those middle-layer tests yourselves at registration time — a substantial undertaking. We'd recommend implementing an already-certified SoC and Host Stack combination instead to avoid this.
decision_logic: Middle protocol layer testing (LL, L2CAP, GAP, GATT, ATT, SM) is structurally dependent on referencing an already-registered SoC/Host Stack combination, since these layers can't be validly tested against a product implementation in isolation — choosing an uncertified chip shifts this substantial testing burden onto the manufacturer.
final_recommendation: When a customer proposes building a product without an already-certified Bluetooth chip, proactively explain the middle-layer testing burden this creates and recommend an already-certified SoC/Host Stack combination as the practical alternative, rather than letting them discover this requirement only once registration is attempted.
risk_if_done_wrong: A customer proceeding with an uncertified chip without understanding the middle-layer testing requirement could face unexpected, substantial additional testing cost and complexity discovered only late in the certification process.
